Dino Correia 10 min read · Nov 4, 2026 -- Listen Share Ask on the screen, ask where they got stuck, skip telemetry and sort what comes in. Short answer: ask inside the product, on the screen the question is about, right after the user has done the thing you want to learn about. Ask one short question that takes a tap (“How easy was it to export your report?”), then an optional “Where did you get stuck?”. Keep a “Help us improve” button in the app for people who want to say more. Then put every piece of feedback, from the widget, email and support, in one list, tag it by theme, and fix the theme that comes up most. Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Michelle Tresemer on Unsplash A small SaaS product often has a few hundred users who log in every day and almost none who say anything. A survey emailed to all of them gets two answers, both “looks good”. The people who do write in send long emails about one thing, and the inbox becomes a second job. Founders keep asking about this on Reddit, in r/SaaS, r/microsaas, r/buildinpublic and r/nocode. Each section below takes one of their questions, in their words, and answers it. How do I get feedback from existing daily active users? Your daily active users are already in the app, so that is where to reach them. An email arrives later, somewhere else, about something they no longer remember clearly. A question on the screen arrives while the experience is fresh, and answering takes a second instead of opening a link and a form. Pick the screens where you know least about how users feel, and ask about that screen only: First run of a feature. On the feature screen, after first use: “How useful is this for you?” (1 to 5) End of onboarding. On the last setup step: “How easy was it to get set up?” (1 to 7) A task that often fails. On the results or confirmation screen: “Did this do what you expected?” (Yes / No) Settings and billing. On the settings or plan page: “Is anything here hard to find?” Anything, any time. A “Help us improve” button in the app menu or a side tab: “What would make this product better for you?” The first four ask about one moment, so every answer is tied to a screen and a task. The button is always there for users who have something to say and would not otherwise know where to say it. How to ask for app feedback that people actually answer? “Do you like the app?” gets polite answers. People who stay with a product mostly like it, or they would have left, and they do not want to sound ungrateful to a small team. “Where did you get stuck?” asks about a fact, not an opinion, and gives them permission to complain. Instead of “Do you like the new dashboard?”, ask “What were you looking for on the dashboard today?” Instead of “Any feedback?”, ask “Where did you get stuck this week?” Instead of “How would you rate our app?”, ask “How easy was it to send your first invoice?” Instead of “What features should we add?”, ask “What did you last do in another tool because you could not do it here?” Questions about what someone just did, or last did, get specific answers. Questions about what they might want in the future often get wish lists that say little about what they would use. One rating question plus one optional comment box is enough. Each extra question loses some of the people who would have answered the first. How do I increase the amount of feedback from users? Change when and how you ask before you ask more often. A common story: a founder with about 100 users prompts for feedback on the site, emails everyone who finished sign-up and everyone who abandoned it, and gets a handful of replies. That is normal. Most users never answer a survey, and the ones who do are not a random sample. Check these first: The question arrives at the wrong time: on login, before the user has done anything, or in an email days later The question is too broad to answer quickly, such as “Tell us what you think” Answering takes too long: a link to a form with ten fields The same users see the question on every visit, even after they answered or closed it Users do not believe anything will happen with their answer For users who signed up and left, a personal email from the founder usually gets more replies than a survey link. Send it within a day or two, ask one question (“What stopped you from finishing setup?”), and make it easy to reply in one line. Expect few replies, and read every one. How do you collect user feedback if telemetry is not possible? Some products cannot track users at all: privacy tools, health and finance apps, tools for journalists, anything people chose because it does not watch them. Others choose not to. Without analytics you lose the “where”, so the feedback has to carry it.
